tasks.title: Rewrite README.md with Comprehensive Documentation
tasks.description: Create a comprehensive README.md that properly documents the repository structure, setup instructions, and architecture overview based on the repository snapshot.
tasks.details:
Create a new README.md with the following sections:
1. Project Overview (name, purpose, tech stack)
2. Quick Start Guide (prerequisites, installation, development commands)
3. Architecture Overview (brief explanation of Nuxt 4 + Content v3)
4. Repository Structure (key directories and their purposes)
5. Content Management (how to add/edit blog posts and pages)
6. Deployment Process

Use the structure from the repository snapshot as a guide. Include code blocks for installation and development commands using pnpm. Add a screenshot of the site if available. Ensure all links are absolute and working.
tasks.testStrategy: Manual review of the README.md for completeness, accuracy, and clarity. Verify all commands work as documented by following the setup instructions on a fresh clone of the repository.

tasks.title: Consolidate Architecture Documentation
tasks.description: Organize and consolidate architecture documentation by creating a permanent architecture overview and preserving migration history.
tasks.details:
1. Create a new directory structure in `/docs/` with the following:
   - `/docs/architecture/overview.md` - Current architecture state
   - `/docs/architecture/history/` - Move migration plans here

2. In the overview.md, document:
   - Content v3 schema design and data flow
   - Component structure and responsibilities
   - Routing strategy (especially dynamic routes)
   - Build and deployment process
   - TypeScript integration

3. Include diagrams if possible (can use Mermaid syntax for GitHub rendering)

4. Update any references to old documentation locations
tasks.testStrategy: Review documentation for technical accuracy. Have another team member attempt to understand the architecture solely from the documentation. Verify all links between documents work correctly.

tasks.title: Audit and Clean Configuration Files
tasks.description: Review and clean up Nuxt and Tailwind configuration files to remove legacy settings and ensure they're optimized for Nuxt 4 and Content v3.
tasks.details:
1. In `nuxt.config.ts`:
   - Verify `compatibilityVersion: 4` is set
   - Remove any deprecated options from Nuxt 2/3
   - Ensure Content v3 module is properly configured
   - Check for optimal build settings for static site generation
   - Verify TypeScript integration settings

2. In `tailwind.config.js`:
   - Update to use the latest Tailwind v6.14.0 features
   - Ensure content paths include all Vue files (`app/**/*.{vue,js,ts}`)
   - Verify theme customizations are working
   - Remove any legacy plugins or configurations

3. In `content.config.ts`:
   - Verify schema definitions match actual content structure
   - Ensure proper typing for all collections
   - Check for any performance optimizations
tasks.testStrategy: Run build process with verbose logging to check for warnings. Test development server startup time. Verify hot module replacement works correctly. Check build output size and optimize if necessary.

tasks.title: Verify and Fix Asset Migration
tasks.description: Ensure all assets used in Markdown content are correctly located in the public directory and referenced via absolute paths.
tasks.testStrategy: Run the verification script and ensure zero errors. Manually check a sample of blog posts in the development environment to verify images load correctly. Test the production build to ensure all assets are correctly included and referenced.

tasks.title: Implement Search Functionality
tasks.description: Implement Nuxt Content v3 search functionality to allow users to search through blog posts and content pages.
tasks.testStrategy: Test search functionality with various queries to ensure it returns relevant results. Verify performance by testing with large content sets. Test edge cases like empty queries, special characters, and very long search terms. Ensure the UI correctly displays loading states during searches. Verify the search component works correctly both in the navigation and on the dedicated search page. Ensure the UI is responsive and accessible.

tasks.title: Enhance SEO Implementation
tasks.description: Verify and improve SEO implementation using Nuxt's useHead and meta tag generation for the new Content v3 schema.
tasks.testStrategy: Use tools like Lighthouse, SEO Checker, and social media debuggers (Facebook, Twitter) to verify meta tags are correctly implemented. Test structured data with Google's Rich Results Test. Verify sitemap.xml is valid and includes all pages.

tasks.title: Update Copilot Instructions for Nuxt 4 and Content v3
tasks.description: Update GitHub Copilot instructions to reference Nuxt 4 and Content v3 patterns, removing any legacy v2 references.
tasks.details:
1. Locate all Copilot instruction files in the repository:
   - `.github/copilot-instructions.md`
   - Any other instruction files in `.github/` or `.gemini/`

2. Update the instructions to reflect Nuxt 4 and Content v3 patterns:
   - Replace references to Nuxt 2 with Nuxt 4 equivalents
   - Update Content module references to use Content v3 API
   - Update component examples to use Composition API
   - Update file path references to match the new directory structure
   - Include examples of proper TypeScript usage

3. Add specific instructions for:
   - Content schema definition in `content.config.ts`
   - Proper use of `queryContent()` and `<ContentRenderer />`
   - Tailwind CSS v6.14.0 usage patterns
   - Pug template usage with Vue 3

4. Merge any separate migration instructions into the main instructions file

5. Add examples of best practices for:
   - TypeScript type definitions
   - Vue 3 Composition API usage
   - Content v3 query patterns
   - Dynamic routing with Nuxt 4
tasks.testStrategy: Have GitHub Copilot generate code based on the updated instructions and verify it follows Nuxt 4 and Content v3 patterns. Test the generated code in the project to ensure it works correctly.

tasks.title: Implement Basic Testing Framework
tasks.description: Set up a basic testing framework to address the lack of automated testing identified in the technical debt section.
tasks.testStrategy: Run the test suite to verify it works correctly. Add tests for at least one core component and one utility function. Verify GitHub Actions runs tests on push and pull requests.

tasks.title: Split blog social image into dedicated OG and thumbnail fields
tasks.description: Introduce a second frontmatter image field for blog posts to separate Open Graph/Twitter share images from small mosaic thumbnails, update components to use the correct field with fallbacks, and document the new convention.
tasks.details:
This task involves refactoring the blog image metadata so that Open Graph/Twitter unfurl images and front-page mosaic thumbnails are served from two distinct frontmatter fields rather than overloading a single socialImage field. Start by updating the Nuxt Content v3 schema in content.config.ts for the blog collection. Locate the existing socialImage field definition (which should currently be an object or string used for OG images) and define a second image object, e.g. thumbnail or mosaicImage, with the same shape as socialImage. The shape should be a nested z.object containing src, mime, width, height, and alt properties, with src configured for Studio media picking via .editor({ input: 'media' }) so that content authors can visually select images. Ensure that both socialImage and thumbnail are optional to preserve backward compatibility, while encouraging new posts to supply both. The socialImage field should be documented and validated as targeting a 1.91:1 ratio at 1200x630 pixels for Open Graph and Twitter cards, while thumbnail should target the existing mosaic grid aspect ratio (approximately 512x332) or rely on consistent CSS cropping in the pinned-post grid.

Next, update app/components/blog/pinned.vue to use the new thumbnail field. Replace direct references to article.socialImage.src in the pinned mosaic with logic that prefers article.thumbnail.src when present and falls back to article.socialImage.src when thumbnail is undefined. Implement this fallback defensively: handle cases where either field is missing by providing a sensible default image URL from the public assets (for example, a generic blog placeholder) and ensure that alt attributes follow the same preference order (thumbnail.alt, then socialImage.alt, then a hardcoded string such as "Blog post thumbnail"). If the component currently assumes certain dimensions, confirm that CSS-based aspect ratio control (e.g. object-fit and fixed container ratio) is robust enough that source image dimensions do not cause layout breakage. Also check that the mosaic rendering still works correctly for older posts that only have socialImage defined.

Then, review app/pages/blog/[...slug].vue and any related SEO composables introduced in the SEO enhancement work. Ensure that OG and Twitter meta tags (og:image, og:image:width, og:image:height, twitter:image) are derived exclusively from socialImage, not thumbnail. When constructing the absolute image URL, continue to rely on public paths (for example, `${siteUrl}${doc.socialImage.src}`), and set width and height meta values to match the frontmatter data or to the canonical 1200x630 defaults when the frontmatter is incomplete. Confirm that the code path for generating meta tags gracefully handles posts that lack socialImage: either fall back to a site-wide default OG image or omit the image tags entirely in a controlled manner. If the SEO composable introduced earlier already centralizes OG/Twitter meta generation, extend it to accept both socialImage and thumbnail inputs but only use socialImage for meta tags.

Once the schema and components are updated, perform a targeted backfill on recent posts where image fields are known to be misaligned, starting with the imagetexter post. For imagetexter, move the existing 512x332 screenshot crop from socialImage into thumbnail and set socialImage to a new 1200x630 image that is appropriate for social sharing, ensuring that the src paths are absolute and point to assets in the public directory. Optionally, repeat this for other recent posts such as dragline, ia-book-page-downloader, and nova-zombie-simulator so that they follow the new convention (large socialImage for OG, smaller thumbnail for mosaic). Older posts can be left as-is initially because the mosaic component will fall back to socialImage when thumbnail is missing, preserving the current behavior. During backfill, verify that YAML frontmatter is syntactically correct and that the new fields are recognized by Nuxt Content.

Finally, update the wiki-blog-conventions documentation (e.g. ~/.claude/skills/wiki-blog-conventions or an equivalent internal doc) to describe the new two-field system. Document that socialImage is mandatory for new posts, with recommended dimensions of 1200x630, high-quality composition, and relevance to the post for OG/Twitter cards, while thumbnail is recommended for controlling how posts appear in the front-page pinned mosaic with a smaller, grid-friendly ratio. Clarify best practices for choosing images, including avoiding text-heavy thumbnails, ensuring that socialImage is not a tiny screenshot better suited for thumbnails, and maintaining consistent alt text for accessibility. Include concise examples of frontmatter blocks showing both fields with realistic values. If Nuxt Content Studio is used, confirm that the new fields appear in the visual editor under sensible labels and ordering, so that authors can reliably set social and thumbnail images without editing raw YAML.
tasks.testStrategy: To validate this task, begin with automated tests using the existing Vitest and @nuxt/test-utils setup. Create unit tests or component tests for app/components/blog/pinned.vue that render the component with different article objects: one containing both socialImage and thumbnail, one with only socialImage, and one with neither image defined. Assert that when both fields are present, the rendered src attribute matches article.thumbnail.src and that alt text prefers thumbnail.alt, while when thumbnail is missing, src falls back to article.socialImage.src. In the case where neither is defined, assert that the component renders a configured default image and alt text, and that it does not throw runtime errors. Use snapshot or DOM-based assertions to confirm that the mosaic layout remains intact across these scenarios. Add tests for the blog slug page, either via composable tests or full-page rendering with nuxt/test-utils. Provide a mock Content document with both socialImage and thumbnail and assert that the generated head/meta object contains og:image and twitter:image tags pointing to the socialImage URL, not thumbnail. Verify that og:image:width and og:image:height meta tags reflect the expected 1200x630 values or the dimensions stored in frontmatter. Include a scenario where socialImage is missing to confirm that the code either uses a site-wide default OG image or omits the image tags, matching the intended behavior. Ensure that the tests run successfully in the Vitest environment and are integrated into the CI pipeline. Beyond automated tests, perform manual validation in a local development environment. Inspect the front page pinned mosaic and confirm that posts with thumbnail defined show the correct, small grid-friendly image, while older posts that only have socialImage still display images via the fallback. Check that there are no visual regressions, broken images, or unexpected aspect ratio distortions. Then open at least one updated blog post (such as imagetexter) and view the HTML source of the page to confirm that the OG and Twitter meta tags reference the socialImage URL and have appropriate width, height, and alt attributes if applicable. Use external tools such as Facebook Sharing Debugger, X/Twitter Card Validator, or an OG checking service to fetch the URL and ensure that the social preview card picks up the new socialImage and not the thumbnail. Finally, verify the documentation and editor experience. Open the wiki-blog-conventions document and ensure that it accurately describes the two-field convention with examples. If using Nuxt Content Studio, open a sample blog post in the Studio and confirm that both socialImage and thumbnail appear as media-selectable fields with clear labels, and that saving changes updates the underlying frontmatter as expected. Optionally, create a new test post following the documented convention and verify end-to-end behavior: the pinned mosaic uses the thumbnail, social previews use the socialImage, and no errors appear in the console during navigation or build. Once all tests pass and manual checks confirm correct behavior, consider this task complete.

tasks.title: Implement GitHub Actions-based Nuxt static deployment to GitHub Pages
tasks.description: Replace the local `pnpm run publish` flow with a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the Nuxt static site and deploys `.output/public` to the `gh-pages` branch via an official GitHub Pages deploy action, triggered manually with `workflow_dispatch`.
tasks.details:
This task focuses on migrating the current manual publish process, which runs `pnpm run publish` locally to clean, generate, and deploy the static Nuxt build, into a fully defined GitHub Actions workflow that performs the same steps in CI and pushes the result to the `gh-pages` branch.[4][11] The existing flow relies on the `gh-pages` npm CLI (`gh-pages -t -d .output/public --nojekyll`) executing on a developer machine with local Git credentials, which introduces friction, machine-specific requirements, and potential drift between what is committed to `main` and what is actually deployed.[4] By introducing a `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` workflow, we centralize deployment logic, ensure reproducibility, and allow deployments to be triggered from any browser via the GitHub Actions UI, while preserving the current "push only when ready" behavior by using the `workflow_dispatch` trigger instead of an automatic `push` trigger.[5][10]

Begin by designing the overall deployment approach based on the current repository expectations for GitHub Pages. Today, GitHub Pages serves from the `gh-pages` branch, with the `gh-pages` CLI pushing the contents of `.output/public` into that branch; to minimize disruption, the first iteration of this workflow should keep that branch-based model and use either `JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action` or `peaceiris/actions-gh-pages` to perform the branch push from CI.[1][16] Both actions are built specifically to take a directory of static files and publish them to a target branch such as `gh-pages`, and they remove the need for the local `gh-pages` CLI while integrating cleanly into GitHub Actions.[1][16] The workflow should live at `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and be named clearly (for example, `Deploy to GitHub Pages`) to make its intent obvious in the Actions tab; this name also appears in the Pages configuration when using the modern artifact-based deployment path, so a descriptive name is helpful if the project later migrates away from the `gh-pages` branch.[5][18]

The workflow needs to be triggered manually using `workflow_dispatch` to preserve the current control model where the site is only updated when explicitly requested, rather than on every push to `main`.[10] In the `deploy.yml` file, set `on: workflow_dispatch` at the top, optionally defining inputs such as an environment label or a boolean flag to control whether tests are run before deployment; however, the initial version can omit inputs for simplicity and just provide a single "Run workflow" button in the GitHub UI.[10] Manual dispatch is appropriate because the repository does not currently use a pull-request-based review gate, so tying deployment directly to `push` would make every typo or experimental commit immediately live, which the requirements explicitly call out as undesirable. If, in the future, the repository adopts a PR review flow and stabilizes its commit practices, the trigger can be extended to include `on: push: branches: [main]` to support fully automatic deployment after merges to `main`, but this should be deferred until the team is comfortable with that level of automation.[5][10]

In the workflow job definition, configure the runner and environment steps necessary to build the Nuxt static site. The job should run on `ubuntu-latest` and perform a standard sequence: check out the repository, set up Node.js, install dependencies, and run the same clean/generate steps that `pnpm run publish` currently performs.[4][11] Use `actions/checkout` as the first step to pull the contents of the `main` branch into the runner; this is required before any deployment action can run, and is also explicitly documented in both the GitHub Pages deploy actions and GitHub’s own examples.[1][2][5] For Node.js, prefer `actions/setup-node` and select a version compatible with Nuxt 4 and the project’s tooling, such as Node 20, which aligns with the Nuxt GitHub Pages deployment example and upcoming GitHub Actions defaults.[11][18] If the project uses `pnpm`, you can either call `pnpm/action-setup` followed by `actions/setup-node`, or use a composite action like `wyvox/action-setup-pnpm` that handles checkout, PNPM installation, caching, and optional Turborepo support for monorepos, thereby reducing workflow boilerplate while still giving you a robust pnpm environment.[8][9]

To improve performance and keep CI times manageable, you should enable dependency caching in the workflow. When using `actions/setup-node`, configure its built-in cache support with `cache: 'pnpm'` (or `cache: 'npm'`/`'yarn'` if the project prefers those), and ensure the cache key includes the lockfile hash so that changes to dependencies automatically invalidate stale caches.[8] This pattern is recommended because it avoids the fragility of caching `node_modules` directly, which can skip `postinstall` scripts on cache hits and cause subtle breaks, especially in Nuxt projects that rely on post-install tooling.[8] If the repository is a monorepo with multiple workspaces, adjust `cache-dependency-path` to cover all `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `package-lock.json` files, ensuring that each workspace’s dependencies are correctly captured.[8][9] These caching steps are strictly optional for the first iteration of the deploy workflow but are strongly recommended to keep deployments fast, especially once the manual trigger is used frequently.

Once Node and dependencies are ready, mirror the existing publish sequence inside the workflow. The current local command `pnpm run publish` appears to run `pnpm run clean && pnpm run generate && pnpm run deploy`, with `deploy` invoking `gh-pages` to push `.output/public` to the `gh-pages` branch.[4] In CI, you should run `pnpm run clean` and `pnpm run generate` exactly as on the developer machine, ensuring the static build output goes to `.output/public` as expected; this preserves behavior across machines and allows simple comparison between local and CI builds if needed.[11][12] If the repo has already migrated to Nuxt 4’s GitHub Pages preset, you may instead use `npx nuxt build --preset github_pages`, which writes a static site to `.output/public` and handles base URL configuration necessary for `https://<user>.github.io/<repository>/` style deployments.[11] The decision of whether to continue using `pnpm run generate` or switch to `nuxt build --preset github_pages` should be guided by the current Nuxt configuration and Task 4’s cleanup work; this task should confirm that the chosen build command is compatible with the project’s Nuxt 4 setup and produces a correct static bundle.[4][11]

For the deploy step, select either `JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action` or `peaceiris/actions-gh-pages` and configure it to take `.output/public` as the publish directory and push it to the `gh-pages` branch.[1][2][16] With the JamesIves action, you specify the target branch and folder via inputs, and the action will create the `gh-pages` branch if it doesn’t exist; this is convenient if the branch may be missing in some environments or if the project later decides to publish documentation from separate branches.[1][2] With `peaceiris/actions-gh-pages`, you define `publish_dir: ./.output/public` and rely on the repo’s default Pages branch, typically `gh-pages`, which the action will populate on each run.[16] In both cases, the action uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication rather than a personal access token, meaning no new secrets are required as long as the workflow and repository grant appropriate permissions; this helps keep credentials secure while allowing the CI job to push commits to `gh-pages`.[16][17]

Critically, the workflow must grant the `GITHUB_TOKEN` write permissions to repository contents so that the deployment action can push to the `gh-pages` branch.[16][17][19] By default, GitHub Actions may run with read-only or minimal permissions depending on the repository’s settings for workflow permissions, and attempting to push without `contents: write` will produce errors similar to those documented in troubleshooting articles about insufficient GITHUB_TOKEN rights.[19] To avoid this, include a `permissions` block in the workflow or specifically in the deploy job that sets `contents: write`; for example, at the job level, you can write `permissions: contents: write` to ensure that all steps in that job can push commits.[16][17][19] Alternatively, you can set repository-wide workflow permissions to "Read and write" under Settings → Actions → General, and then rely on the default token behavior; however, using job-level permissions is more precise and aligns with GitHub’s guidance that workflows should grant the minimum necessary access.[17][19]

The GitHub Pages configuration must continue to point to the `gh-pages` branch after this change so that GitHub’s Pages service uses the branch populated by the new workflow.[4][6][20] In the repository settings, under the "Pages" section within "Code and automation", verify that the build and deployment source is set to "Deploy from a branch" and that the branch dropdown specifies `gh-pages` with the correct folder (usually `/`, meaning the branch root).[6][20] If the project ever chooses to adopt the modern artifact-based deployment flow using `actions/upload-pages-artifact` and `actions/deploy-pages`, the Pages source would instead be set to "GitHub Actions" and the workflow would upload the static site as an artifact and deploy it to the `github-pages` environment, but that is outside the scope of this initial branch-based task.[3][5][18][20] For now, you should confirm that the existing `gh-pages` branch remains untouched until the first CI deployment succeeds, as recommended by migration guides, and then verify that GitHub Pages serves the new content correctly from that branch.[18]

Concurrency is another consideration, although less critical for a manually triggered workflow. If there is any risk that multiple deploy runs might overlap, perhaps due to multiple collaborators clicking "Run workflow" in quick succession or a misconfigured automatic trigger added later, you can add a `concurrency` block to the workflow or deploy job that ensures only one deployment runs at a time and cancels or queues subsequent runs.[2][15][16] Marketplaces and documentation for deploy actions note that overlapping deployments can cause conflicts in writing to the `gh-pages` branch, and concurrency controls help prevent such overlaps by grouping deployments under a shared key (for example, `concurrency: group: pages-deploy-main cancel-in-progress: true`).[2][15][16] For the first iteration, this can be optional, but it is useful to document the pattern in the workflow comments so that it can be enabled if the deployment frequency increases.

As a final part of this task, update local scripts and documentation so that the deployment single source of truth is the GitHub Action rather than `pnpm run publish`. The `pnpm run publish` script can either be removed to avoid confusion or retained as an emergency fallback with clear documentation that CI is the preferred path; in either case, the docs in `/docs/architecture/overview.md` describing the build and deployment process should be updated to reflect that the standard deployment path is now the `Deploy to GitHub Pages` workflow triggered from the Actions tab.[3][5] This documentation should mention the manual trigger behavior, the fact that the workflow builds from the latest `main` branch, and the continued use of `gh-pages` as the Pages source so that future contributors understand how the site is shipped. Aligning the workflow, configuration files cleaned in Task 4, and the architecture documentation reduces the risk of divergence between code, CI, and prose, which is particularly important for static site deployments that may be maintained over long periods.[3][4]

Example `deploy.yml` content for this task, adapted to Nuxt and `pnpm`, could look like the following, which you should tailor to the project’s exact scripts and Node version:

```yaml
name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Clean build output
        run: pnpm run clean

      - name: Generate static site
        run: pnpm run generate
        # or: npx nuxt build --preset github_pages

      - name: Deploy to gh-pages
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v4
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: ./.output/public
```

This configuration encapsulates the existing publish behavior inside CI, uses the `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `contents: write` to push to `gh-pages`, and exposes a single manual trigger entry point in the GitHub Actions UI, which satisfies the requirement to keep deployment under explicit human control while moving execution off the local developer machine.[1][5][10][16][17][19]
tasks.testStrategy:
To validate this task, begin by creating or updating `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` with the steps described above and committing it to the `main` branch, then navigate to the repository’s **Actions** tab and confirm that a workflow named "Deploy to GitHub Pages" appears with a "Run workflow" button, indicating that the `workflow_dispatch` trigger is correctly recognized.[5][10] Click "Run workflow" to start a deployment and watch the job logs, verifying that `actions/checkout` successfully checks out the `main` branch, `actions/setup-node` installs the expected Node.js version, `pnpm` installs dependencies without error, and the `clean` and `generate` steps complete, producing a `.output/public` directory on the runner.[1][4][5][11] Next, inspect the deploy step using `JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action` or `peaceiris/actions-gh-pages` and ensure it runs without authentication errors; if there are errors about insufficient permissions on `GITHUB_TOKEN`, confirm that the workflow’s `permissions` block includes `contents: write` or that repository-wide workflow permissions are set to "Read and write", and re-run the workflow until the deploy completes successfully.[16][17][19]

After a successful deploy run, open the repository’s **Settings → Pages** section and verify that the build and deployment source is configured to "Deploy from a branch" with branch `gh-pages` and the expected folder (usually `/`), which confirms that GitHub Pages is still serving from the branch populated by the new workflow rather than expecting an artifact-based deployment.[4][6][20] Check the `gh-pages` branch itself to ensure that its contents have been updated by the workflow, paying attention to the presence of the generated static files and, if applicable, an empty `.nojekyll` file that some deploy tools add to ensure Jekyll processing is bypassed; while the deploy actions typically handle this automatically, verifying the branch contents helps confirm that the CI-based publish step replicates the behavior of the previous `gh-pages` CLI command.[4][16] Once the branch looks correct, visit the live site at `https://<username>.github.io/<repository>/` and confirm that the content matches the latest `main` branch, including any recent changes made to Nuxt components, Content v3 content, or Tailwind styling, all of which were validated in Task 4.[4][6][11][20]

To further test reliability, make a small, visible change in the repository (for example, adjusting a headline or adding a marker comment in a page), commit it to `main` without running any local publish scripts, and then manually trigger the deploy workflow again from the Actions tab.[5][10] Confirm that the new change appears on the live site only after the workflow completes and does not appear if you simply push to `main` without running the workflow, which demonstrates that deployment is now entirely controlled by the CI workflow rather than local commands. Repeat this process a few times to ensure that successive runs do not conflict and that the `gh-pages` branch reflects each deployment accurately; if needed, enable `concurrency` in the workflow and verify that overlapping runs are either queued or cancelled, ensuring a predictable deployment sequence.[2][15][16] Finally, review `/docs/architecture/overview.md` and any other project documentation describing the build and deployment process to ensure they now refer to the GitHub Actions-based deployment and the manual "Run workflow" procedure rather than `pnpm run publish`, then have another contributor follow the documented steps end-to-end to confirm that they can trigger a successful deployment from a clean machine without local Node or pnpm installed.[3][4][5][10] This combination of CI log inspection, branch verification, live site checks, and documentation-based usability testing provides strong confidence that the manual publish step has been correctly and comprehensively migrated into a GitHub Action.
